items.title: 1.4.1 Polar Coordinate System of a Complex Number

source_refs.note: Book pp. 15-16: printed heading "1.4.1 Polar Coordinate System of a Complex Number" (number repeated), figure, polar form, cis Note, Example 12, Note on x = 0, Principal Argument

blocks.text: 1.4.1 Polar Coordinate System of a Complex Number

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints this heading as 1.4.1, a number it already used for “Properties of Cube Roots of Unity” (book page 12). We keep the printed number so you can find it in your textbook; only the numbering is wrong.

Consider the adjoining diagram. The complex number \(z = x + iy\) is shown as the point \(A\) in the Argand plane. Join \(O\) to \(A\) and drop the perpendicular \(AM\) on the \(x\)-axis. In the right triangle \(OMA\) the hypotenuse is \(OA = r\) and the angle at \(O\) is \(\theta\), so
\[\cos\theta = \dfrac{x}{r},\quad \sin\theta = \dfrac{y}{r}\]
From the diagram, therefore,
\[x = r\cos\theta \quad\text{and}\quad y = r\sin\theta\]
where \(r = |z|\) is the modulus and \(\theta\) is called an argument of \(z\).

blocks.alt: Argand plane with origin O. The point A(r, theta) represents z = x + iy. The segment OA has length r = |z| = square root of (x squared + y squared) and makes angle theta with the x-axis. AM is perpendicular to the x-axis, with OM = x = r cos theta and AM = y = r sin theta.
blocks.caption: Figure: the complex number z = x + iy as the point A(r, θ); x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text:
Hence
\[x + iy = r\cos\theta + i\,r\sin\theta \quad \text{(i)}\]
that is, \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\), where
\[r = |z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\]
\[\theta = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{y}{x}\quad (x \ne 0)\]
Equation (i) is called the polar form of the complex number \(z\).

blocks.text_alt: z equals r times open bracket cos theta plus i sin theta close bracket

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why use the polar form? The rectangular form \(x + iy\) tells you "how far across and how far up". The polar form tells you "how far from O and in which direction". In 1.3.3 you will see that multiplying and dividing complex numbers is much easier in polar form: multiply the distances and add the angles.
Converting:
• polar to rectangular: \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\).
• rectangular to polar: \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\), and \(\theta\) from \(\tan\theta = y/x\) with the correct quadrant (see Principal Argument below).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: We can write \(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta = \operatorname{cis}\theta\), so the polar form is also written \(z = r\operatorname{cis}\theta\).

blocks.title: Example 12
blocks.problem: Express the complex number \(1 + i\sqrt{3}\) in polar form.
steps:
Given: \(z = 1 + i\sqrt{3}\), so \(x = 1\) and \(y = \sqrt{3}\).
To find: \(r\) and \(\theta\) such that \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\).
Method: the real part equals \(r\cos\theta\) and the imaginary part equals \(r\sin\theta\). Squaring and adding gives \(r\); dividing gives \(\tan\theta\); the signs of \(x\) and \(y\) fix the quadrant.

Step I: match the real and imaginary parts
The book prints: Put \(r\cos\theta = 1\) and \(r\cos\theta = \sqrt{3}\). The second equation must use sine (see the Book correction below):
\[r\cos\theta = 1 \quad \text{(1)}\]
\[r\sin\theta = \sqrt{3} \quad \text{(2)}\]
Why: \(r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = r\cos\theta + i\,r\sin\theta\); two complex numbers are equal when their real parts are equal and their imaginary parts are equal.

Step II: find r
Square (1) and (2) and add:
\[r^2\cos^2\theta + r^2\sin^2\theta = 1 + 3\]
\[r^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) = 4\]
\[r^2 = 4\]
\[r = 2\]
Why: \(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\) removes \(\theta\). We take \(r = 2\), not \(-2\), because \(r = |z|\) is a distance. (The book writes this directly as \(r^2 = 1^2 + (\sqrt{3})^2\).)

Step III: find θ
Divide (2) by (1):
\[\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{1} = \sqrt{3}\]
\[\theta = \tan^{-1}\sqrt{3} = 60^{\circ}\]
Why: \(x = 1 > 0\) and \(y = \sqrt{3} > 0\), so the point is in the first quadrant, where \(\tan^{-1}\) gives the right angle directly. \(60^{\circ} = \pi/3\).

Step IV: write the polar form
\[1 + i\sqrt{3} = 2\cos 60^{\circ} + i\,2\sin 60^{\circ}\]
\[= 2(\cos 60^{\circ} + i\sin 60^{\circ})\]
\[= 2\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{\pi}{3}\]
Why: put \(r = 2\) and \(\theta = 60^{\circ}\) into \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Example 12, Step I, the book prints “Put \(r\cos\theta = 1\) and \(r\cos\theta = \sqrt{3}\)”. The second equation should be \(r\sin\theta = \sqrt{3}\), because the imaginary part of \(r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\) is \(r\sin\theta\). The rest of the book's solution (\(r = 2\), \(\theta = 60^{\circ}\)) is correct.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text:
• If \(x = 0,\ y > 0\) then \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
• If \(x = 0,\ y < 0\) then \(\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
• If \(x = 0,\ y = 0\) then \(\theta\) is undefined.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why this Note? When \(x = 0\) the formula \(\tan^{-1}(y/x)\) cannot be used, because we cannot divide by zero. So we read the angle from the picture: a point on the positive imaginary axis (for example \(2i\)) points straight up, angle \(\pi/2\); a point on the negative imaginary axis (for example \(-3i\)) points straight down, angle \(-\pi/2\). The number \(0\) is the pole itself: it has no direction, so it has no argument.

Principal Argument: the principal argument \(\theta\) of a complex number \(z = a + bi\) is the angle between the positive real axis and the line joining \((a, b)\) to the origin in the Argand plane. The book writes it as
\[\arg z = \theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)\]
It is denoted by \(\arg\). It is a single, specific value of the argument, chosen in the standard range
\[\arg z \in (-\pi, \pi]\]

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
\(\tan^{-1}(b/a)\) alone can give the wrong angle. A calculator's \(\tan^{-1}\) only returns angles between \(-\pi/2\) and \(\pi/2\), so it is correct only when \(a > 0\) (the point is to the right of the imaginary axis).
For \(z = -1 - i\): \(b/a = 1\) and \(\tan^{-1} 1 = \pi/4\). But \(-1 - i\) is in the third quadrant, while \(\pi/4\) points into the first quadrant. The true principal argument is \(-3\pi/4\).
The reason: \(\dfrac{-1}{-1}\) and \(\dfrac{1}{1}\) are the same number, so \(b/a\) "forgets" the signs of \(a\) and \(b\). Always look at the signs to find the quadrant first.

How to find the principal argument correctly (our method):
1. Look at the signs of \(a\) and \(b\) and decide the quadrant (or axis) of \(z\). A quick sketch helps.
2. Find the reference angle \(\alpha = \tan^{-1}\left|\dfrac{b}{a}\right|\), an acute angle between \(0\) and \(\pi/2\).
3. Use the table below to get \(\theta\) in \((-\pi, \pi]\).

blocks.caption: Teaching table (ours): the principal argument of z = a + bi, with α = tan⁻¹|b/a|

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Practice with the table (our illustrations, not textbook examples):
• \(z = -1 + i\): Quadrant II, \(\alpha = \pi/4\), so \(\arg z = \pi - \pi/4 = 3\pi/4\).
• \(z = -1 - i\): Quadrant III, \(\alpha = \pi/4\), so \(\arg z = -(\pi - \pi/4) = -3\pi/4\).
• \(z = 1 - i\): Quadrant IV, \(\alpha = \pi/4\), so \(\arg z = -\pi/4\).
• \(z = -\sqrt{3} - i\): Quadrant III, \(\alpha = \tan^{-1}(1/\sqrt{3}) = \pi/6\), so \(\arg z = -5\pi/6\).
• \(z = -4\): negative real axis, \(\arg z = \pi\).

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text:
Why the range \((-\pi, \pi]\)? Any argument can be changed by a full turn \(2\pi\) without moving the point, so \(z\) has infinitely many arguments \(\theta + 2k\pi\) (\(k\) an integer). Choosing the range \((-\pi, \pi]\) picks exactly one of them. \(\pi\) is included (it is the direction of the negative real axis) and \(-\pi\) is left out, so the negative real axis gets only one value.
Angles above the real axis get positive principal arguments (\(0\) to \(\pi\)); angles below it get negative ones (\(0\) to \(-\pi\)).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
• \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\), so \(z = x + iy = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = r\operatorname{cis}\theta\).
• \(r = |z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) is the modulus; \(\theta\) is an argument of \(z\).
• On the imaginary axis: \(\theta = \pi/2\) (above) or \(-\pi/2\) (below); \(z = 0\) has no argument.
• The principal argument \(\arg z\) is the one argument in \((-\pi, \pi]\).
• Find the quadrant first, then use \(\alpha = \tan^{-1}|b/a|\) and the table.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
• Writing \(r\cos\theta\) for the imaginary part (the slip printed in Example 12). The imaginary part is \(r\sin\theta\).
• Taking \(r\) negative. The modulus \(r = |z|\) is never negative.
• Using \(\tan^{-1}(b/a)\) without checking the quadrant when \(a < 0\).
• Giving a principal argument outside \((-\pi, \pi]\), for example \(5\pi/3\) instead of \(-\pi/3\).
